segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Quantum computing is a somehow a very new subject for my show after 270 plus episodes, but before we get into the field itself,

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'm wondering what originally drew you to it as a as a research area? Was it in the physics or the computer science side or the conceptual weirdness?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, so so I mean my background is in computer science and math. Uh it's not at all physics. Uh you know the the physics that I've learned I've sort of picked up on the streets so to speak, but I first heard about quantum computing when I was a teenager in the the the mid 1990s. So you know Shor's algorithm for factoring I think had just recently been discovered and I read a popular article about it that said you know well that this this mathematician has shown that a a quantum computer could factor you know huge numbers by just trying every possible divisor in a different parallel universe, right? And I remember my reaction at the time which is you know this sounds like garbage. This sounds like you know the physicists just do not understand what they're up against, right? Um you know like it it can't work that way, right? You know that would be too good to be true and and and and if that was true then you know why would you even need to work hard to figure that out, you know? You know then then that just seems right and so then but then you know I I had to read read more about it to be sure, so I I um um um over a summer that I spent at Bell Labs in I I I think 1998 I did my my my my my boss was nice enough to to say you know sure spend a month to just you know read up on quantum computing and you know do a report about it and you know there were there were already then websites explaining it and I remember just being amazed that you know when when you when you actually learn what quantum computing is you know it's just linear algebra, right? It's just vectors. It's just you know you don't even need to know just about anything about physics, right? You need to know you need to understand the certain generalization of the rules of probability themselves that involves complex numbers and you know once you once you learn that then you can understand how the basic quantum algorithms work. So I learned about Shor's algorithm, I learned about Grover's algorithm for searching giant databases which had also recently been discovered. You know and then I realized that Lov Grover worked in the same building as me that he was the discoverer of Grover's algorithm, right? And so I went to talk to him and you know and I had ideas for how to improve Grover's algorithm that were just complete nonsense. They just didn't work at all. Okay, but Grover was very very nice and he said well why don't you do an internship with me next summer. So I did that and and that was where I I met students of of Umesh Vazirani at Berkeley who were then kind of at the forefront of figuring out what quantum computers could or couldn't do, you know not just for one or two specific problems but for like you know whole whole classes of problems. And and I really wanted to learn whatever these people knew, right? I you know I wasn't sure that I could do anything original in quantum computing and at the time I was also very interested in AI. So I wasn't I wasn't sure what I would go into you know and actually when I applied to grad school I did get into Berkeley, but it was the AI people who recruited me there. And so I so I I went there thinking that maybe I would do AI, maybe I would combine AI with quantum computing somehow. Then it was only after my first year at Berkeley that I really fell in with the quantum computing people and that was that was 25 years ago. But I mean what what attracted me was first of all you know that that this was relatively new. There was this low hanging fruit, you know there were like very very basic questions that still weren't answered that I thought you know maybe I could answer. And secondly that you know you you could actually answer these questions using math, right? We had you know a very well defined model of what a quantum computer is. I mean you know this was decades ahead of you know the experiment catching up, but you know now today you know the experiments finally are catching up to the theory, but in some sense they are merely you know confirming the theory in every particular, right? They're not you know you know they're they're we haven't had any surprises about the basic physics of it. And so so you know because we knew the mathematical model of what a quantum computer is you know we could prove theorems, you know you don't you know about what quantum computers would and wouldn't be able to do. And so that was that was appealing to me. You know and then and then also just the fact that the like the most basic questions of computer science like what are the limitations of efficient algorithms, you know does P equal NP, you know things like that were somehow coming together with you know the most basic some of the most basic questions in physics right you know what is quantum mechanics actually saying about reality, right? And you know and that and and it seemed like well something interesting has to come out from that from that intersection. So you know those were the things that drew me to it you know more than 25 years ago. I think those are those are the things that you know are still appealing to me about it today. And you know you might notice what I didn't mention is sort of the the practical prospect of solving you know problems faster, you know which which is never been the main motivation for me, right? If if we do manage to you know get quantum computers that we can use for practical applications I mean to me that's just icing on the cake.
